title: About Yolanda "Yo" Butler
description: The story of Yolanda "Yo" Butler: 30+ years as an entrepreneur, 13+ years at Operation HOPE, and the philosophy behind The Business of You.
text: Yo About Yo A life spent building, and helping others build. Entrepreneur, coach and speaker Yolanda "Yo" Butler on the road that shaped The Business of You. Yolanda "Yo" Butler · Antioch, California Her story I know the road, because I've walked it. For more than thirty years I've been an entrepreneur. I ran Christian Family Preschool in Oakland for thirteen years and grew a consignment business alongside it. I learned what it takes to make payroll, earn a family's trust and keep the doors open through hard seasons. Then I spent my career helping other owners do the same. I trained women entrepreneurs at Women's Initiative for Self Employment. I advised small business owners at the Contra Costa SBDC. And over thirteen years at Operation HOPE, I grew from Small Business Coordinator to VP Community Relations to Financial Well-Being Coach. "We build the business around you , not the other way around." Along the way I saw the same thing again and again: good people with good ideas, held back by money stress, missing connections or a plan that didn't fit their life. The Business of You is my answer. Strategy, financial wellness and community, shaped around the person doing the building. — Yo The journey Three decades, one mission. Founder Christian Family Preschool, Oakland Ran her own preschool for 13 years and grew a consignment business on the side. Trainer Women's Initiative for Self Employment Trained women entrepreneurs to plan, launch and grow their businesses. Advisor Contra Costa SBDC Advised small business owners on planning, funding and growth. 13+ years Operation HOPE Grew from Small Business Coordinator to VP Community Relations to Financial Well-Being Coach. Education Cal State East Bay Studied Business Administration and served as president of the Black Business Association. The Business of You™ philosophy Four beliefs behind every talk. I Start with the person A business should fit the life of the person building it. We begin with your strengths, story and season. II Financial dignity Credit, money management and wealth that lasts. Everyone deserves to understand their money. III Each one, reach one Social capital is real capital. When you rise, you reach back and bring someone with you. IV Wellness is strategy A rested, confident founder makes better decisions. Mental wellness is part of the business plan. "Your story, your skills and your relationships are assets. Build on them. " Yolanda Butler For event planners & media Bios & headshots. Copy the bio that fits your program, or download it as a text file. The headshot is cleared for event and press use. title: How to Know If Your Business Idea Solves a Real Problem
description: Before you spend a dollar, run three simple tests: name the exact person with the problem, measure how much it hurts, and look for proof that people will p
text: ¶ Business · 6 min read How to Know If Your Business Idea Solves a Real Problem By Yolanda "Yo" Butler · November 4, 2026 A business idea solves a real problem when you can name the exact person who has it, show that it costs them time, money or peace of mind, and find proof that they will pay to fix it. If any of those three is missing, keep testing before you build. Why do so many good ideas fail? In more than thirty years of running and advising businesses, I have watched talented people pour their savings into ideas nobody asked for. The idea was clever. The person behind it was capable. But the problem was either too small, too vague, or belonged to people who would never pay to solve it. That is why the first step of The Business of You framework is simply this: identify your problem. Everything else, from pricing to funding to marketing, is easier when the problem is real. Who exactly has this problem? "Everyone" is not a customer. Write one sentence describing a specific person: their role, their situation and the moment the problem shows up. "Busy parents" is vague. "A single mom who runs a home daycare and spends every Sunday night doing paperwork" is a person you can find, talk to and serve. How much does it really hurt? Ask that person what the problem costs them today. Look for answers measured in hours, dollars, stress or missed opportunities. The bigger and more frequent the pain, the stronger the business. How often does the problem happen? What do they do about it now? What does the current fix cost in time or money? What happens if it never gets solved? Will anyone pay to solve it? Interest is not the same as payment. The strongest signal is someone who has already paid for a partial solution, or who asks how soon they can buy yours. Offer a simple version, a pre-order or a pilot, and see who says yes with their wallet. "If people will not pay for the small version, they will not pay for the big one." What should you do next? Talk to ten people who fit your one-sentence description this month. Ask about their problem, not your idea. Take notes on the words they use, because those words become your marketing later. Then decide: build, adjust or move on. All three are wins, because each one saves you from guessing. title: Business Credit Basics: 7 Steps Before You Apply for a Loan
description: Separate your finances, register the business properly, build a payment history and organize your documents months before you ask a lender for anything.
text: ¶ Financial wellness · 7 min read Business Credit Basics: 7 Steps Before You Apply for a Loan By Yolanda "Yo" Butler · November 4, 2026 Before applying for a business loan, separate your personal and business finances, make your business official, build a record of on-time payments, and gather the documents lenders ask for. Starting three to six months early gives you time to fix problems instead of explaining them. This article is education, not financial or legal advice. For your specific situation, talk with a licensed professional or a trusted lender. Why does business credit matter? Business credit helps lenders, suppliers and partners see whether your company pays its bills reliably. A strong profile can open better terms and protect your personal credit from carrying the whole business. During my years at Operation HOPE, the owners who prepared early walked into the bank with confidence instead of dread. What are the seven steps? Separate your money: open a business bank account and run every business dollar through it. Make it official: register your business properly and get an employer identification number (EIN). Use consistent details: the same business name, address and phone number everywhere. Start small with vendors: some suppliers offer terms and report payments, which helps build history. Pay early or on time, every time: payment history matters more than almost anything else. Keep clean books: a simple monthly profit and loss statement and bank reconciliation. Check your personal credit too: many small business lenders still look at it. Which documents do lenders ask for? Requirements vary, but most lenders ask for some combination of business and personal tax returns, recent bank statements, a profit and loss statement, a balance sheet, your business registration and a short explanation of how much you need and how you will repay it. How do you tell your funding story? Numbers open the door, but your story keeps it open. Be ready to explain in two minutes what your business does, who pays you, what the money is for and how it will help you repay. Practice it out loud. Confidence is built by preparation, not by luck. "Lenders are not looking for perfect. They are looking for prepared." title: Social Capital: Why Your Network Is a Business Asset
description: Relationships open doors money cannot. Map the people your business needs, give before you ask, and follow up like it matters, because it does.
text: ¶ Business · 5 min read Social Capital: Why Your Network Is a Business Asset By Yolanda "Yo" Butler · November 4, 2026 Social capital is the value of your relationships: the people who know your work, trust you and will open a door when you need it. It is a real business asset because referrals, partnerships, funding and first customers almost always come through people before they come through ads. What does "each one, reach one" mean? It is a simple idea I have lived by: when you rise, you reach back and bring someone with you. Communities grow stronger when every person lifts one more. In business, that generosity comes back as trust, introductions and opportunities you could never buy. Which relationships does a business need? A mentor who has walked the road ahead of you Peers at your stage to trade lessons with A banker or lender who knows your name Connectors who introduce you to the right rooms Customers who become your loudest advocates How do you build a network without feeling awkward? Start by giving. Share a resource, make an introduction, or celebrate someone else's win. Ask for advice rather than favors; people love to help when they feel useful. And follow up: a short thank-you note after a conversation is rare enough to be remembered. How do you keep relationships alive? Keep a simple list of the people who matter to your business and reach out to a few each week, with no agenda but care. Relationships are like savings. Small, steady deposits grow into something you can count on. "Your next opportunity is probably one conversation away." text: § Trust How Agent Yo works. Agent Yo is an AI assistant. Here is what it does, what it does not do, and how your conversation is handled. title: Accessibility Statement
description: Accessibility statement for The Business of You: our WCAG 2.2 AA goal, the features we provide, known limitations and how to request help.
text: § Trust Accessibility statement. Everyone should be able to use this site. Here is what we do, and how to tell us if something gets in your way. Our goal We aim to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. What we do Text and buttons meet AA color contrast. Gold is used for decoration, never for small text on light backgrounds. Every page works with a keyboard, with visible focus outlines and a "Skip to content" link. Images have text descriptions, and forms have labels and clear error messages. Animations turn off automatically when your device is set to reduce motion. Pages use real headings and landmarks for screen readers. Known limitations Podcast episodes and videos will include transcripts and captions at launch. Some older PDFs or third-party embeds may not yet meet every guideline. Tell us If anything on this site is hard to use, email hello@yourdomain.com and tell us the page and what happened. We will respond within two business days and provide the information in another format if you need it. Questions? Email hello@yourdomain.com or use the contact page .
